questions.title: A vision for small-business banking
questions.prompt: You have just joined as head of product for a small-business banking app. The teams are shipping features but cannot say where the product is going. Create a three-year product vision and show how it changes what teams do next quarter.
hints: What will a small-business owner's financial life look like in three years?
What insight do incumbents miss?
How does a vision become a roadmap without becoming a feature list?
followups: The CEO likes it but asks what you will stop doing. Answer.
How will you know in a year whether the vision is right?
Two teams' current projects do not fit. What happens to them?
criteria: Grounded in customer insight, not technology trends.
Memorable and specific enough to guide choices.
Connected to near-term bets and explicit stops.
Includes signals that would show the vision is wrong.
Plans how to roll it out to teams.
outline: Research: interviews, data on where owners spend time on money tasks.
Insight: owners do not want banking; they want cash-flow certainty with less admin.
Vision: 'the business runs its money on autopilot, and the owner always knows what is safe to spend'.
Pillars: automatic bookkeeping; cash-flow forecasting; getting paid faster.
Next quarter: bets per pillar; stop projects that do not serve them.
Signals: forecast accuracy, admin time saved, retention of owners.
questions.reference:
I would start with customers, not the roadmap: interview owners and look at where their time goes. A likely insight is that owners do not want ‘banking’; they want to know what money is safe to spend and to spend less time on admin.

Vision: “The business runs its money on autopilot, and the owner always knows what is safe to spend.” Three pillars: bookkeeping that happens automatically from transactions; cash-flow forecasting that warns before a shortfall; and getting paid faster. It guides choices: a feature that does not reduce admin or uncertainty is not a priority.

Next quarter it changes work: one team starts automatic categorisation, another a simple 30-day cash forecast, a third invoice reminders; two projects that serve none of the pillars stop, and I would explain why to those teams personally. I would watch forecast accuracy, admin time reported by owners and retention; if owners do not trust forecasts after a year, the vision needs revisiting.

questions.title: Sixty engineers, four products
questions.prompt: You lead four products with about sixty engineers. One is mature and profitable, one is growing fast, one has been struggling for two years, and one is a new bet. The CFO asks you to justify your allocation. What do you propose?
hints: What role does each product play in the company's strategy?
What evidence would make you fund or stop the struggling product?
How much should the new bet get, and what must it prove?
followups: The struggling product's team is excellent. Does that change your answer?
The mature product's revenue dips 5%. Do you move people back?
How often do you rebalance?
criteria: Classifies investments by role (core, growth, bet) and allocates deliberately.
Uses evidence and explicit criteria to fund or stop.
Sets milestones and kill criteria for the bet.
Protects the core without starving growth.
Rebalances on a cadence and communicates clearly.
outline: Roles: core cash generator, growth engine, struggling, new bet.
Allocation (illustrative): core ~30%, growth ~45%, bet ~15%, struggling ~10% pending decision.
Struggling product: 90-day decision with criteria (retention, pipeline); merge, pivot or sunset.
Bet: small team, milestones (customer validation, paid pilots), kill date.
Cadence: quarterly review; communicate reasons to teams.
questions.reference:
I would start by stating each product’s role. The mature product funds the company: it needs reliability and efficient improvements, not maximum headcount. The growing product is where returns on people are highest now. The new bet needs a small, strong team and clear milestones. The struggling product needs a decision, not another year of moderate funding.

An illustrative allocation: about 30% on the mature product, 45% on the growing one, 15% on the new bet, and 10% on the struggling product for one quarter while we decide. For the struggling product, I would set criteria — retention, sales pipeline, strategic value — and in 90 days merge it, pivot it or sunset it. An excellent team is a reason to move them to a better problem, not to keep funding a weak product.

The new bet gets milestones — validated customer problem, paid pilots — and a date by which it must show them. I would review the allocation every quarter on evidence, not on a single month’s revenue, and explain the reasons to every team.

questions.title: Teams organised by layer
questions.prompt: Your product organisation is split into a front-end team, a back-end team and a data team. Every customer-facing feature needs all three, and delivery is slow. How would you redesign the organisation, and how would you make the change?
hints: What should a team be able to deliver on its own?
What stays shared, and who owns it?
What could go wrong during the transition?
followups: Engineering leadership disagrees. How do you work it out?
How do you keep standards consistent across the new teams?
How will you know the reorganisation worked?
criteria: Diagnoses the problem as handoffs between layers.
Proposes teams aligned to customer problems with the skills to deliver end to end.
Keeps a platform team for truly shared capabilities.
Plans the change with engineering leadership, communication and support.
Measures success (cycle time, outcomes, engagement).
outline: Diagnose: every feature crosses three queues; nobody owns outcomes.
Design: cross-functional teams per customer problem; a small platform team.
Decision rights: teams own their area's roadmap and metrics.
Change: co-design with engineering leaders; explain why; move people with care; transition period.
Standards: guilds or chapters for disciplines.
Measure: lead time, goal attainment, engagement survey.
questions.reference:
The slowness is structural: every feature waits in three queues, and no team owns a customer outcome. I would move to cross-functional teams, each aligned to a customer problem — say onboarding, payments, reporting — with the front-end, back-end and data skills to deliver end to end. A small platform team keeps truly shared capabilities such as the design system and the data platform.

I would not do this alone: engineering and design leadership co-own the design, because they manage most of the people. We would explain the reasons openly, let people express preferences, keep managers stable where possible and plan a transition with clear ownership for in-flight work.

To keep quality consistent, disciplines meet regularly across teams with shared standards. Success: time from idea to launch, teams meeting their outcome goals, and engagement scores during and after the change. If engineering leaders disagree, I would understand their concern — often on-call or career paths — and adapt the design.

questions.title: A strong PM who is struggling
questions.prompt: One of your product managers was excellent on a small product but is struggling after being moved to a larger, more political area. Their team is frustrated. What do you do?
hints: What specifically is going wrong?
What support has the PM had?
When is it fair to change the role?
followups: After two months of coaching, little has changed. Now what?
The PM asks to go back to their old area. How do you respond?
How do you prevent this in future moves?
criteria: Gathers specific evidence from several sources.
Gives direct, specific feedback.
Provides coaching and support with clear expectations and time frame.
Considers the fit of the role, not just the person.
Acts fairly and promptly if things do not improve.
outline: Gather facts: team feedback, stakeholder feedback, outcomes.
Conversation: specific behaviours and impact; listen.
Plan: goals for 60 days; coaching on stakeholder mapping and escalation; pair with a peer.
Check in weekly; adjust scope if needed.
If no improvement: change role (possibly back to a smaller scope) respectfully.
Prevention: transition plans for moves.
questions.reference:
First I would understand what ‘struggling’ means: talk to the team and key stakeholders, look at decisions and outcomes. Often a PM who thrived with a small team keeps doing everything themselves and has not learned to work through stakeholders.

Then a direct conversation with specific examples and their effect, and listening — they may be missing context or support. Together we set clear goals for about two months: for example, a stakeholder map, a weekly decision forum, and a roadmap agreed with the two most important partners. I would coach weekly and pair them with a peer who has run a similar area.

If after that period things have not improved, the kind thing is to change the role — possibly back to a scope where they were excellent — framed honestly as fit, not failure. For future moves, I would plan transitions: clear expectations, an introduction to stakeholders and early check-ins.
pitfalls: Waiting for it to fix itself.

questions.title: Missing the annual target
questions.prompt: Halfway through the year, your product area is clearly going to miss its annual revenue target by about 20%. You present to the executive team next week. What do you say, and how do you prepare?
hints: What do executives need: explanation, a new forecast, or a decision?
How much of the miss is controllable?
Who should hear this before the meeting?
followups: The CEO asks whether you should have seen this earlier. Answer.
The CFO wants the original target kept. How do you respond?
What would you not say?
criteria: Leads with the new forecast and the decision needed.
Explains causes honestly, separating controllable from external.
Brings recovery options with costs.
Pre-wires key executives.
Takes ownership and proposes earlier warning systems.
outline: Headline: new forecast, range, confidence.
Causes: controllable vs external, with evidence.
Options: recovery plays and their cost and probability.
Recommendation and decision needed.
Pre-wire CEO and CFO.
Owning it: what you missed and what changes.
questions.reference:
I would start with the headline: “We will finish the year about 20% below target; the forecast range is X to Y.” Then the causes, separated honestly into what we controlled — a launch that slipped, a pricing change that underperformed — and what we did not — a market slowdown. Executives trust people who make that split clearly.

Then options: two or three recovery plays with what they cost, what they would recover and how likely they are; and a recommendation, including whether to reset the target. I would be explicit about the decision I need.

Before the meeting, I would brief the CEO and CFO individually so nobody is surprised in the room. On ‘should you have seen it earlier?’, I would answer directly — what the early signals were, why they were missed, and the leading indicators we now review monthly. I would not blame other teams or present a recovery plan I do not believe.
pitfalls: Surprising the CEO in the room.

questions.title: Teams pulling against each other
questions.prompt: In your marketplace, the buyer team is measured on conversion and the seller team on number of listings. Listings have grown fast, but buyers complain about low-quality items and conversion is falling. Redesign the goal system.
hints: What is the shared outcome both teams serve?
What does each team's metric encourage at the other's expense?
How do you keep metrics a team can actually move?
followups: The seller team says quality is not their job. Respond.
How do you set targets without a baseline?
How often should the metric tree change?
criteria: Identifies the shared outcome (successful transactions, buyer and seller satisfaction).
Builds a metric tree linking team inputs to it.
Replaces volume with quality-adjusted metrics.
Adds cross-team guardrails.
Plans review cadence and protects definitions.
outline: Shared outcome: completed transactions with good experiences on both sides.
Tree: transactions = buyers × conversion; conversion depends on relevant, quality listings.
Seller team: quality listings that sell (sell-through), not listing count.
Buyer team: conversion with guardrails on returns and complaints.
Shared guardrails: buyer satisfaction, seller earnings.
Cadence: quarterly review; single owner for definitions.
questions.reference:
The two metrics conflict: listing count rewards volume, including low-quality items, which hurts buyers and therefore conversion. I would anchor both teams on the shared outcome: completed transactions where both sides are satisfied.

Then build the metric tree: transactions depend on active buyers and conversion; conversion depends on relevant, good-quality listings. The seller team’s goal becomes sell-through rate of new listings (listings that sell within 30 days), not count; the buyer team keeps conversion with guardrails on returns and complaints. Both teams share guardrails: buyer satisfaction and seller earnings.

Without baselines, I would set the first quarter as measurement, then set targets. The tree is reviewed quarterly, but definitions are owned centrally and change rarely, so teams can trust the trends. If the seller team says quality is not their job, the new metric makes it their job — and gives them a goal they can move.
pitfalls: Adding more metrics without resolving the conflict.

questions.title: Convincing another division
questions.prompt: As a principal PM, you believe the company should unify its two separate checkout systems, owned by two divisions. Neither division reports to you. How do you make it happen?
hints: What does each division gain or lose?
What evidence would persuade them?
What is the smallest first step?
followups: One division's leader is openly against it. What do you do?
When would you escalate to the executive team?
How do you keep momentum once agreed?
criteria: Understands each division's incentives.
Builds a fact-based case in their terms.
Starts with a small, visible win.
Builds allies and shared ownership.
Escalates as a last resort, with options.
outline: Interview leaders: goals, pains with current checkout.
Case: duplicate cost, inconsistent customer experience, conversion gap — with data.
Proposal: shared component first (e.g. payment methods), not full merge.
Allies: engineering leads, finance, customer support.
Governance: joint ownership; escalate only if blocked on company priority.
questions.reference:
I would start by understanding each division: what they are measured on and what they fear — usually losing control of a system tied to their revenue. Then I would build a case in their terms: the duplicated engineering cost, the conversion gap between the two checkouts, and customer complaints about inconsistency.

Rather than proposing a full merger, I would suggest a first shared piece both divisions want — for example, adding new payment methods once instead of twice. A visible win builds trust. I would find allies: engineering leads tired of duplicate work, finance, support. The proposal should become a joint plan with shared ownership, not mine.

If one leader remains opposed after that, I would ask what evidence would change their mind. Only if the disagreement is truly about company priorities would I take it to the executive team — with options and the cost of doing nothing, not a complaint.

questions.title: Stopping something you started
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you stopped a product or project that you had championed.
hints: What evidence made you stop?
How did you tell the team?
What happened to the people?
followups: Did you wait too long?
How did leadership react?
What did you salvage?
criteria: Clear, evidence-based decision.
Overcame personal attachment.
Handled people with care.
Salvaged learnings or assets.
Changed how they set kill criteria.
outline: What you championed and why.
The evidence that it was not working.
The decision and how you made it.
Communication and care for the team.
What was salvaged.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “I championed a marketplace for third-party templates. After nine months, supply was healthy but buyers rarely returned. I compared it with the milestones we had set and recommended stopping. I told the team first, in person, explained the data and made sure each person had a new role they wanted. We kept the template engine, which later powered our onboarding. Now every bet I sponsor starts with written kill criteria and a review date.”
